abstract: Structural policy and social practices, including redlining and white flight, have driven disinvestment and heightened exposure to persistent environmental pollutants resulting from residual impacts of industrial activity. Urban agriculture, meant to empower and feed communities, are frequently established on vacant lots that may contain these contaminants and pose a threat to human health. To circumvent the legacy of contaminations on bare soil, Chicago growers are using raised beds to create a barrier between contaminated soil and healthier imported compost. Our goal was to assess the efficacy of this barrier system by 1) quantifying eight heavy metals and Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) between existing soils and raised beds, 2) examining the difference between key soil properties, and 3) determining the environmental risk determined by their potential ecological risk index (PERI). We expected that metal concentrations would vary across sites and soil types, and raised beds would have fewer heavy metals than existing soils. Our results showed existing soils generally had higher levels of heavy metals with significant differences in lead and arsenic, suggesting that raised beds could be a viable barrier system. We also found higher levels of phosphorus, nitrogen, and magnesium in raised beds than existing soils. Thirdly, lead and copper significantly increased with pH while arsenic and copper decreased with organic matter levels. Despite the presence of heavy metals, the sites had a lower risk of environmental contamination, indicating that growers' extra measures to ensure their soils are safe to grow food may be sufficient, barring metal- and site-specific strategies.
